column1: What are the three components of a Kolmogorov probability space, and what role does each play?
column2: $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$: $\Omega$ is the sample space of all possible outcomes; $\mathcal{F}$ is a σ-algebra of measurable subsets (events) of $\Omega$; $P$ is a probability measure assigning values in $[0,1]$ to events in $\mathcal{F}$, satisfying countable additivity and $P(\Omega)=1$.

column1: Why can't we always assign a probability measure to every subset of an uncountable sample space like $[0,1]$?
column2: The Vitali construction (1905), using the Axiom of Choice, produces subsets of $[0,1]$ to which no translation-invariant measure can be consistently assigned. This forces restriction to a σ-algebra $\mathcal{F} \subsetneq 2^\Omega$ rather than the full power set.

column1: State the three defining closure properties of a σ-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ on $\Omega$.
column2: 1) $\Omega \in \mathcal{F}$; 2) Closure under complementation: $A \in \mathcal{F} \implies A^c \in \mathcal{F}$; 3) Closure under countable unions: $A_1, A_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{F} \implies \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \in \mathcal{F}$.

column1: What measurability condition must a function $X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy to qualify as a random variable?
column2: For every Borel set $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the preimage $X^{-1}(B) = \{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \in B\}$ must belong to $\mathcal{F}$, ensuring $P(X \in B)$ is well-defined via the pushforward measure $P_X$.

column1: Why does a continuous random variable assign zero probability to any single point?
column2: Because Lebesgue measure assigns zero measure to singleton sets, and probabilities for continuous r.v.s are computed as integrals of a PDF over intervals ($P(X \in [a,b]) = \int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx$); integrating over a point yields zero.

column1: List the four defining properties of a cumulative distribution function (CDF) $F_X(x)$.
column2: 1) Non-decreasing; 2) Right-continuous; 3) $\lim_{x\to-\infty} F_X(x) = 0$; 4) $\lim_{x\to\infty} F_X(x) = 1$. Discrete r.v.s produce jump discontinuities equal to PMF values; continuous r.v.s produce absolutely continuous CDFs.

column1: How is the marginal density $f_X(x)$ recovered from a joint density $f_{X,Y}(x,y)$?
column2: By integrating out the other variable: $f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy$. Geometrically this projects the joint density surface ('shadow') onto the $x$-axis; formally it is an instance of the disintegration theorem.

column1: Give the formula for the conditional density $f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)$ in terms of the joint density.
column2: $$f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}, \quad \text{defined wherever } f_X(x) > 0.$$ This is Bayes's ratio applied to densities, encoding the probabilistic update upon learning $X=x$.

column1: Why does a joint distribution carry strictly more information than its collection of marginal distributions?
column2: Marginals discard the dependence structure between variables — many distinct joint distributions can share identical marginals while differing in correlation/dependence; the 'surplus' information beyond the marginals is precisely this dependence structure.

column1: Define almost sure convergence $X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X$ precisely.
column2: For almost every outcome $\omega \in \Omega$ (i.e., with probability 1), the real-number sequence $X_n(\omega)$ converges classically to $X(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$: $P(\{\omega : \lim_{n\to\infty} X_n(\omega) = X(\omega)\}) = 1$.

column1: How does convergence in probability differ from almost sure convergence?
column2: Convergence in probability ($X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$) only requires $P(|X_n - X| > \varepsilon) \to 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ as $n \to \infty$ — it permits exceptional sets of outcomes that change with $n$, whereas almost sure convergence requires a single fixed exceptional set of probability zero across all $n$. A.s. convergence implies convergence in probability, but not conversely.

column1: What does $L^p$ convergence, $X_n \xrightarrow{L^p} X$, require, and what is its special case at $p=2$?
column2: It requires $\mathbb{E}[|X_n - X|^p] \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. At $p=2$ this is mean-square convergence, favored in engineering due to its connection with orthogonal projections in Hilbert spaces (e.g., minimum variance unbiased estimators).
